summary: Reviewed the dvpwa (aiohttp) application: the DAO layer, request handlers (views.py), auth utilities, middlewares, Jinja2 setup, routes, forms, config and templates. The app is deliberately vulnerable and the review confirms several real, reachable flaws: an unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create, global disabling of Jinja2 autoescaping leading to stored XSS, disabled CSRF protection, unsalted MD5 password hashing, session cookies without HttpOnly, and missing authorization on state-changing endpoints. Overall risk is critical (remote, unauthenticated SQL injection). Coverage is the whole Python codebase and relevant templates/config; static JS/CSS assets and SQL migration data were not deeply reviewed for logic.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create via student name
findings.description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement by interpolating the raw student name with Python string formatting instead of using a parameterized query. The name reaches this sink unsanitized from the POST /students/ handler (views.py:57, data['name']), and that handler performs no authentication check, so any anonymous remote user can inject arbitrary SQL. A payload like ') ; DROP TABLE ...-- or a subquery in the value breaks out of the quoted VALUES clause, allowing data exfiltration/modification. Every other DAO method in this repo correctly uses driver parameterization (%s / named params); this is the single injectable sink.
findings.evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})  -> cur.execute(q)  with name = request.post()['name'] from views.students (POST /students/, no auth). Contrast Review.create/Mark.create which pass params to cur.execute.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized execution: q = "INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)" and await cur.execute(q, {'name': name}); never build SQL with % string formatting on user input.

findings.title: Stored XSS from globally disabled Jinja2 autoescaping
findings.description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so no template output is HTML-escaped. User-controlled values stored via unauthenticated/low-privilege endpoints are rendered verbatim, giving persistent XSS. For example a course review submitted at POST /courses/{id}/review (Review.create, review_text) is rendered unescaped at course.jinja2:22 ({{ review.review_text }}); student names (students.jinja2:16) and course title/description are likewise unescaped. An attacker stores <script>...</script> once and it executes in every visitor's browser (including admins).
findings.evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=..., context_processors=[...], autoescape=False); rendered sink course.jinja2:22 {{ review.review_text }} with review_text taken from request.post() in views.review -> Review.create.
findings.recommendation: Enable autoescaping (autoescape=True, the Jinja2 default) and only mark specific trusted values safe; do not disable escaping globally.

findings.title: CSRF protection disabled (csrf_middleware not registered)
findings.description: A working CSRF-checking middleware exists (middlewares.csrf_middleware) and templates emit a _csrf_token, but the middleware is commented out of the application's middleware list, so no POST request is ever validated for a CSRF token. Combined with the session cookie being sent automatically, an attacker can forge cross-site POSTs to state-changing endpoints (create student/course, submit reviews, evaluate/assign marks, logout) on behalf of an authenticated victim.
findings.evidence: middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware]; csrf_middleware defined at middlewares.py:26-38 is never applied.
findings.recommendation: Register csrf_middleware in the middleware chain and enforce token validation on all state-changing (POST) requests.

findings.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5
findings.description: User.check_password compares the stored hash to md5(password). Passwords are therefore stored as unsalted MD5 digests, which are extremely fast to brute-force and trivially reversible via rainbow tables if the users table is disclosed (e.g. through the SQL injection above). The equality comparison is also non-constant-time. This weakens credential confidentiality for all accounts.
findings.evidence: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()  -- pwd_hash column populated as MD5, no salt, no KDF.
findings.recommendation: Use a slow, salted password hash (bcrypt/scrypt/argon2) via a vetted library and a constant-time comparison; migrate existing hashes on next login.

findings.title: Session cookie set with HttpOnly disabled
findings.description: The Redis session storage is created with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable by client-side JavaScript. Given the stored-XSS exposure (autoescape disabled), an attacker's injected script can read document.cookie and exfiltrate the session identifier to hijack authenticated (including admin) sessions. There is also no Secure/SameSite hardening.
findings.recommendation: Set httponly=True (the default) and additionally enable secure=True and an appropriate SameSite policy for the session cookie.

findings.title: Missing authorization on state-changing endpoints (evaluate, create student/course, review)
findings.description: The evaluate handler assigns marks to a student for a course with no authentication or admin check, even though the UI only exposes the evaluate form to admins (course.jinja2 gates it behind auth_user.is_admin). Any anonymous user can POST /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id} to forge grades. The same missing-check pattern applies to POST /students/ (Student.create, views.py:54-57) and POST /courses/ (Course.create, views.py:86-90) and POST review (views.py:119-129), none of which use the authorize() decorator that exists in utils/auth.py. The evaluate endpoint is the clearest instance because access is server-side unenforced while presented as admin-only.
findings.evidence: @template('evaluate.jinja2') async def evaluate(request): ... await Mark.create(...) with no @authorize/@authorize(ensure_admin=True); compare authorize() defined in utils/auth.py:12 and only applied to logout.
findings.recommendation: Apply the authorize()/authorize(ensure_admin=True) decorator to all state-changing handlers according to the intended privilege level; do not rely on template-level UI gating for access control.
